--- title: "Statistical learning" subtitle: "STA 363 | Meeting 1" author: "Dr. Lucy D'Agostino McGowan" footer: "[Dr. Lucy D'Agostino McGowan](https://lucymcgowan.com) | STA 363 | figures from *ISLP* (James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani and Taylor, 2023)" logo: "img/icon.png" format: revealjs: theme: [default, custom.scss] slide-number: c/t show-slide-number: all chalkboard: true menu: true preview-links: true code-overflow: wrap code-line-numbers: false highlight-style: github title-slide-attributes: data-color: "#d5008f" execute: echo: true warning: false message: false editor: source jupyter: python3 --- ## Outline ::: {.incremental} * Supervised learning * Notation * Reducible and irreducible error * Flexibility and interpretability ::: # Supervised learning {.center} ## Supervised learning ::: {.takeaway} Given predictors we can measure, estimate a response we cannot. ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.nonincremental} * Labs today $\rightarrow$ readmission within 30 days * Square footage, age, zip $\rightarrow$ sale price * Yesterday's returns $\rightarrow$ tomorrow's direction ::: ::: ## Wage data ![](img/islp/fig1_1.png){fig-align="center" width="88%"} ::: {.source} ISLP Figure 1.1. Wage against age, year, and education for 3,000 men in the Atlantic region. ::: ## Smarket data ![](img/islp/fig1_2.png){fig-align="center" width="88%"} ::: {.source} ISLP Figure 1.2. Previous days' percentage change in the S&P 500, split by whether the market rose or fell the next day. ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.question} These boxplots look nearly identical. Is this a useless data set? ::: ::: ## NCI60 data ![](img/islp/fig1_4.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"} ::: {.source} ISLP Figure 1.4. Sixty four cancer cell lines, 6,830 gene expression measurements each, summarized into two dimensions. ::: # Notation {.center} ## Response and predictors {.small} ::: {.definition} $Y$ is the **response**, also called the outcome or target. $X = (X_1, X_2, \dots, X_p)$ are the **predictors**, also called features. $n$ is the number of observations and $p$ the number of predictors. ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.question} In the `Wage` data, what is $Y$? What is $p$? ::: ::: ## Notation in code {.small} ::: {#53b2e6be .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} DATA = "https://lucymcgowan.github.io/sta-363-f26/data/" Wage = pd.read_csv(DATA + "Wage.csv") Wage[["age", "year", "education", "wage"]].head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
age year education wage

1 24 2004 4. College Grad 70.476020

``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {#2281e472 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} Wage.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (3000, 11) ``` ::: ::: ::: ## The model ::: {.vcenter} $$Y = f(X) + \varepsilon$$ ::: ## The error term ![](img/islp/fig2_2.png){fig-align="center" width="84%"} ::: {.source} ISLP Figure 2.2. Left: observed income and years of education for 30 people. Right: the true $f$ in blue, with the black segments showing each $\varepsilon_i$. ::: # Prediction and inference {.center} ## Prediction and inference :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Prediction Is $\hat{Y}$ close to $Y$? $\hat{f}$ may be a black box. ::: {.fragment .fade-in} ::: {.takeaway} **This course.** ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Inference How does $Y$ change with $X_j$? $\hat{f}$ must be interpretable. ::: {.fragment .fade-in} ::: {.dim} STA 112 and STA 312. ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Reducible and irreducible error ::: {.vcenter} $$E\left(Y - \hat{Y}\right)^2 = \underbrace{\left[f(X) - \hat{f}(X)\right]^2}_{\text{reducible}} + \underbrace{\text{Var}(\varepsilon)}_{\text{irreducible}}$$ ::: ## Irreducible error {.small} ::: {.incremental} * Predictors we did not measure * Predictors we cannot measure * Genuine randomness ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.question} Can we shrink $\text{Var}(\varepsilon)$ by collecting more rows? ::: ::: # Flexibility {.center} ## The true f ![](img/islp/fig2_3.png){fig-align="center" width="54%"} ::: {.source} ISLP Figure 2.3. Income as a function of education and seniority, simulated so that the true surface is known. ::: ## Linear fit ![](img/islp/fig2_4.png){fig-align="center" width="54%"} ::: {.source} ISLP Figure 2.4. A linear model fit by least squares to the data of Figure 2.3. ::: ## Smoothing spline ![](img/islp/fig2_5.png){fig-align="center" width="54%"} ::: {.source} ISLP Figure 2.5. A smooth thin plate spline fit to the same data. ::: ## Overfit spline ![](img/islp/fig2_6.png){fig-align="center" width="54%"} ::: {.source} ISLP Figure 2.6. A rough thin plate spline with zero error on the training data. ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.question} Zero training error. Is this the best model? ::: ::: ## Parametric and non-parametric {.small} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Parametric Assume a form for $f$, estimate a fixed number of parameters. $f(X) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \dots + \beta_p X_p$ Wrong if the form is wrong. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Non-parametric No assumed form. The data pick the shape. Flexible, and needs far more data. ::: :::: ## Flexibility and interpretability ![](img/islp/fig2_7.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"} ::: {.source} ISLP Figure 2.7. The trade off between flexibility and interpretability across methods. ::: ## Regression and classification :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Regression $Y$ is quantitative. Wage. Price. Blood pressure. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Classification $Y$ is qualitative. Readmitted or not. Which digit. ::: :::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.question} Is predicting a zip code regression or classification? ::: ::: # Course mechanics {.center} ## Course structure ::: {.incremental} * Wednesday and Friday: a new method, then you use it * Most Wednesdays: a paper check-in at the start of class * Most Fridays: a problem set due * Three exams: October 9, November 11, and finals week ::: ## Software {.small} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="52%"} ::: {.nonincremental} * `numpy` and `pandas` * `matplotlib` * `scikit-learn` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="48%"} ::: {.nonincremental} * `ISLP` for the book's data * `torch` from November ::: ::: :::: ## Application exercise 1 ::: {.takeaway} Identifying $Y$, $X$, $n$, and $p$, and sorting problems into prediction and inference. ::: ## Before Friday ::: {.nonincremental} * Read ISLP Section 2.2.1 * Have Python running ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.question} How would you check whether the overfit spline was any good? ::: :::
